catalog_quote: Pour les tons, j'ai l'impression que subsistaient certains tons étymologiques des racines du bantu commun ou du A 70 commun. Les tons grammaticaux et syntaxiques présentent un problème non résolu : j'ai l'impression — toujours des impressions ! — qu'il y a jusqu'à un certain point coalescence de faits accentuels et de faits tonaux. Je suis en tout cas à peu près sûr que la syllabe accentuée des mots empruntés à l'anglais porte régulièrement un ton haut. Il semble surtout qu'il y ait fuite devant les paires minimales homophones distinguées seulement par le ton, soit qu'on évite d'employer un des mots, soit qu'on le fasse entrer dans une locution complexe.

new_statements.translation: As for tones, my impression is that certain etymological tones of Common Bantu or Common A 70 roots survived. Grammatical and syntactic tones present an unresolved problem: my impression — always impressions! — is that there is, up to a point, a coalescence of accentual and tonal facts. In any case I am fairly sure that the stressed syllable of words borrowed from English regularly carries a high tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The pidgin keeps (some) lexical tone inherited from the A 70 source languages; stress and tone are said to partly merge, and the only concrete rule given is that the stressed syllable of an English loanword surfaces with high tone. No placement rule for word stress in native vocabulary is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author flags all tone/stress remarks as impressions from three informants plus his own usage, and says speakers avoid minimal pairs distinguished by tone alone (e.g. mbay 'elephant tusk' vs 'palm nut' replaced by compounds mbay-alen / mbay-zok).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (loanwords and lexical roots); observations are impressionistic, no citation-form vs phrase distinction is drawn. The language is a trade pidgin; Alexandre also stresses it shades by degrees into Coast English on one side and imperfectly spoken Bulu/Ewondo on the other.
new_statements.identity_note: Alexandre describes the variety under the names 'bulu des chauffeurs', 'bulu bediliva', 'ewondo populaire', 'pidgin ewondo' (Reyburn) and his preferred 'pidgin A 70'; Glottolog's ewon1240 'Ewondo Populaire' (Guthrie A.70A) is the same entity — a trade pidgin of the Beti-Bulu (A 70) group used on roads, markets and towns of South Cameroon, data from Yaoundé informants (a Vute driver, a Bamileke driver, a Tupuri/Banana soldier) c. 1962. Not to be confused with Ewondo proper (ewon1239).

sources.note: p. 579: consonant and vowel inventories reduced; etymological root tones of Common Bantu / Common A 70 seem to survive, grammatical and syntactic tones an unresolved problem; the author has the impression of a partial coalescence of accentual and tonal facts, and is nearly certain that the stressed syllable of English loanwords regularly carries a high tone; speakers avoid tone-only minimal pairs. No statement of where stress falls in native words.
